r: Senior Seminar is a capstone requiring students to write a paper of publishable quality and present a seminar based on in-depth original research or state-of-the-art practice in technical writing, media, or video production. Drafting research prose is among the most AI-exposed tasks in the evidence base, and writing productivity studies show large gains from AI assistance. But the course's instrumental purpose is a mentor-verified act of original synthesis defended live before an audience -- an oral presentation component that is embodied and interpersonal, and a publishable-quality bar that demands close instructor scrutiny of authenticity and rigor a plausible-but-derivative AI draft cannot satisfy. That verification burden and the live-defense format together drop the rating a band at 24 months, even though the underlying writing task itself is already highly automatable. Rating Low.

By 2031, AI will draft fluent, well-organized research prose competently enough that the composition task itself is substantially automated, consistent with task-exposure research ranking writing among the most positively exposed activities and with productivity studies showing large quality and speed gains. The instrumental case for a student personally producing every sentence of the capstone paper erodes accordingly. What resists automation is the mentor-verified originality of the argument and the live seminar defense, where an instructor must judge whether a student genuinely understands and can defend the work -- a verification-heavy, partly embodied act the jagged-frontier literature suggests AI involvement makes riskier without expert oversight. That dampens the base rise to Medium rather than High. No general-studies designation or foundational role otherwise constrains the course.

A decade out, AI research-writing capability will likely make full first-draft generation of a publishable-quality paper routine, and the central case has most capstone-level composition tasks performed competently by AI with limited human drafting input. Even so, the seminar's defining requirement -- a live, orally defended demonstration that the student authored and understands original work -- is not a task AI performs on the student's behalf, and verifying that understanding remains a human-judgment act with a real error cost if an unearned credential is certified. That keeps the rating at Medium rather than High even as writing automation matures further. The genuine uncertainty is how capstone assessment is redesigned around ubiquitous AI drafting, not whether some form of verified, defended original work remains required.
JMP 4790.d: This course gives the advanced student an opportunity to write a paper of publishable quality and present a seminar based on in-depth research or an application of state-of-the-art practices in an area of Technical Writing and Editing, Media Production, Video Production or other field.

r: Social Documentary has students produce photo/essay projects -- independently or in teams -- that use image and text together to document communities and cultural change for publication and portfolios. The core work is fieldwork: locating subjects, building trust to photograph real people and places, and making in-the-moment compositional and ethical judgments, activities task-exposure research does not classify as automatable and that sit outside the writing- and office-task categories where observed AI usage concentrates. Generative image models can synthesize convincing photographs, but they cannot perform the embodied act of documenting an actual community, which is the course's instrumental purpose. The accompanying text component is more exposed, but it is secondary to the field practice. At 24 months the requirement to personally undertake documentary fieldwork is essentially unaffected by AI capability.

By 2031, AI image generation will be markedly more capable and could plausibly fabricate plausible-looking documentary-style photographs, sharpening a real tension for photojournalism as a market -- an industry-economics question this rating excludes. Whether a student still needs to conduct embodied fieldwork -- locating subjects, earning access, and making real-time ethical and compositional choices in the field -- is unchanged, since that competence is not one a generative model performs on the student's behalf. Verification also matters: authenticating that documentary work reflects real people and events requires human judgment, a concern echoed in jagged-frontier findings about AI's unreliability and mis-calibrated trust outside well-defined tasks. Embodiment keeps the instrumental case Low across this horizon; the surrounding photojournalism market's exposure is a separate question entirely.

Over a decade, synthetic imagery will be pervasive and often indistinguishable from photographs of real events, and the honest caveat is that the market for documentary and editorial photography could be substantially reshaped by that capability, consistent with wide uncertainty about creative-industry disruption generally. Even so, the specific competence Social Documentary builds -- a student personally conducting field research, engaging real subjects, and exercising in-person ethical judgment about representation -- is not a task AI performs for the learner; base automatability rises only modestly here because embodiment is the point, not an incidental feature. The most plausible ten-year shift is in how authentication practices for documentary work evolve, not in whether learning the embodied fieldwork itself remains a necessary, personally acquired student competence. The rating holds Low with continued confidence.
JMP 4890.d: Students create photos/essays for publication and portfolios working independently or in teams. Emphasis is placed upon producing stories and images that deal with cultural definitions that impact social change. Finished work emphasizes the marriage between text and image.
